title: Migraine: Acute Treatment and Prophylaxis Ladder

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with migraine: acute treatment, prophylaxis options and doses, medication-overuse headache, pregnancy and contraception cautions, using NICE CG150 and the SIGN 155 quick reference guide.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Triptan doses (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan oral) and the naproxen dose are not stated in the SIGN quick reference guide, and NICE CG150 gives no doses; they are not listed here.

Prophylactic titration schedules and dosing frequency are not stated in the sources opened; candesartan 16 mg, propranolol 80 to 160 mg, amitriptyline 25 to 150 mg, topiramate 50 to 100 mg and flunarizine 10 mg are daily totals as printed.
Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antibody and botulinum toxin doses, and atogepant and rimegepant doses, are not given.
No Saudi guideline was opened. The Saudi MOH formulary and neurology society guidance were not checked.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: NICE recommends an oral triptan combined with an NSAID or paracetamol for acute migraine, or monotherapy by preference. Overuse of acute headache medication for 3 months or more can cause medication-overuse headache; treatment is withdrawal of all overused drugs for at least 1 month. Chronic migraine is headache on 15 or more days a month for more than 3 months. Topiramate carries developmental and malformation risks and is not for women of childbearing potential unless pregnancy prevention conditions are met.

physicalSigns: Normal neurological examination in uncomplicated migraine (no focal signs).
redFlags: Sudden-onset headache reaching maximum intensity within 5 minutes.
New neurological deficit, cognitive dysfunction, personality change or impaired consciousness.
Head trauma in the past 3 months.
Headache triggered by cough, valsalva, sneezing or exercise; orthostatic headache.
Symptoms suggesting giant cell arteritis or acute narrow-angle glaucoma.
precipitants: Menstruation (menstrual-related migraine: from 2 days before to 3 days after the start of menstruation in at least 2 of 3 cycles).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Headache developed or worsened with regular use of acute medication for 3 months or more.

references.title: NICE CG150: Headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management

clinicalManagement.title: Screen for red flags and diagnose
actions: Apply the red flag list; use a diary for at least 8 weeks.

clinicalManagement.title: Acute treatment
actions: Oral triptan plus an NSAID or paracetamol, or monotherapy; aspirin 900 mg or ibuprofen 400 mg (600 mg if ineffective) or paracetamol 1,000 mg.
Consider an antiemetic; metoclopramide or prochlorperazine 10 mg; do not offer ergots or opioids.

clinicalManagement.title: Prophylaxis ladder
actions: Propranolol 80 to 160 mg daily or topiramate 50 to 100 mg daily after discussion of risks; amitriptyline 25 to 150 mg at night; candesartan 16 mg daily; flunarizine 10 mg daily.
Do not offer gabapentin; up to 10 acupuncture sessions over 5 to 8 weeks if others are unsuitable; riboflavin 400 mg once a day may help some people.

clinicalManagement.title: Address medication overuse
actions: Withdraw overused acute drugs for at least 1 month; do not use prednisolone routinely.

clinicalManagement.title: Specialist options
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After 3 or more oral prophylactics have failed
actions: CGRP monoclonal antibodies for chronic migraine; botulinum toxin A for chronic migraine only, by trained clinicians under neurology.

learningObjectives: Treat the acute attack early with triptan plus NSAID or paracetamol.
